title: Appendix C: Security, Privacy, and Cost Review

sections.title: Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

html:
The main chapters go deep on capacity, state, and recovery, and they leave three other constraints at the edge of the page. Security, privacy, and cost can each stop a design that works from reaching production, and each yields to the same discipline the rest of the book uses: state the assumption, name the evidence, say who owns it, and record what happens if it is wrong.

Use this appendix to identify security, privacy, and cost questions during a design review. Record unresolved questions and assign them to the relevant security, legal, or finance specialist.

Security

We start with authorization, asking where it is checked. A check at the edge is not enough. The resource itself should verify that the authenticated actor, taken from trusted request context, may touch that particular record, because a well-formed identifier can belong to another customer (Chapters 3 and 13). Calls between services deserve the same care: they should authenticate a service identity, and a network address is not one.

Next, find what fails open. Every authorization, rate-limit, and feature-flag lookup has a failure mode. If the authorization service is slow, does the caller allow the request or deny it? The fallback depends on what the request does and which unsafe action the check is meant to prevent. The team must document that decision and test the refusal path.

Then look at credentials. List the ones each service stores and what each would allow an attacker to do if it leaked. Scope them to the smallest set of resources that works, and rehearse rotation before you need it (Chapter 6). The same thinking applies to everything a service accepts without validation: queue messages, events, webhooks, model output, and retrieved documents are all inputs, and each needs validation of structure and authority, as Chapter 13 described for tool calls.

Two more places need attention. The build artifact should specify its base images and dependencies by fixed digest or version, and someone should know who can publish to the registry (Chapter 6). Recovery tooling needs care too, because replay tools, manual status overrides, and emergency allocations are privileged operations, and they should leave audit records naming the actor and the operation (Appendix A).

Identity and Permission Review

For each public API, document the authenticated principal, the resources they can access, and the operation the request may perform. A scope in an access token grants a category of access, but resource ownership may require an additional database lookup. Tenant IDs supplied in URLs or JSON cannot replace that check. Record who approved exceptions and when they expire.

For service calls, identify the workload credential and the permissions available if it is compromised. For asynchronous jobs, identify which human or service authorized the operation, whether that approval can expire or be revoked, and what the worker verifies before the external action. For a deployment, verify the authorized artifact digest and configuration revision at enforcement time. The validation result and the final deployment decision are different audit events.

The review should also examine rate limits on authentication endpoints, failed authorization attempts, secret rotation procedures, and the path for emergency access. A business-logic denial should be distinguishable from a service outage in the operational telemetry.

Choosing Permission Rules

A role is an efficient starting point for a stable capability such as orders:read or refunds:create. It cannot establish which merchant’s orders the employee can access. That requires a resource relationship, such as an active merchant membership, or a policy based on the resource and the request. RBAC supplies broad capabilities, while ABAC can evaluate resource and request attributes. A service may combine the two without introducing a separate policy engine. The choice depends on how frequently permissions change, which services need the decision, and how a denied action will be explained and audited.

For a refund, the review should identify the actor, merchant, payment, action, maximum permitted amount, and applicable approval policy. It should also state whether revocation applies to operations already accepted for later execution. An authorization decision without its resource and time scope is difficult to reuse safely. The same issue appears in deployment approvals that are valid for one image digest and configuration revision but are later applied to another.

Negative Tests at Trust Boundaries

Successful sign-in and a successful refund test are insufficient to verify authorization. The test suite should also exercise these cases:

These tests belong in integration and recovery testing because a correct gateway configuration cannot compensate for a missing resource check inside the owning service. Denials should produce audit evidence without exposing tokens or confidential request data in logs. A rising 403 rate may reflect an authorization attack, a policy change, or an application defect. Monitoring should preserve enough context to investigate those possibilities without including customer IDs as high-cardinality metric labels.

Privacy and the Life of Personal Data

The most useful privacy exercise is to follow one piece of personal data from the moment it enters the system to every place a copy ends up. The primary database is only the beginning. Copies appear in caches, search indexes, event logs, analytics stores, feature stores, training sets, backups, and logs, and most privacy defects live in the copies that never reached the diagram.

Logs and traces deserve particular suspicion, because request bodies, tokens, and identifiers end up in them easily and they have their own retention. Customer identifiers belong in access-controlled records, not in metric labels (Chapter 8). For every store, record its retention period and access policy. A backup may contain personal data that was deleted from the live database after the backup was taken. If that backup is later restored, the recovery procedure must account for deletion requests processed in the meantime before the restored data is made available again. Chapter 7 explains why the restore environment and reconciliation steps must be tested together.

Deletion is the hardest part, because a request to delete has to reach every derived copy. Chapters 11, 12, and 13 each created one: a projection, an event log, a feature store, a training set. For each one, define how a deletion reaches it and which record shows that the deletion was applied. The same goes for location. Regional rules and contracts limit where data may be processed (Chapter 14), and the limit includes third-party processors and inference providers, which receive whatever the prompt contains.

Cost

Cost is a design constraint in the same sense that latency is. A design that meets every objective at ten times the affordable price has failed, and the financial effect may not appear until a later reporting period.

The useful unit is the cost of one completed customer outcome. Cost per call understates it, because outcomes often need several calls. The multipliers to look for are the ones this book has already named: retries, fan-out, cache misses, repeated tool calls, recovery reserves, and telemetry volume.

Consider the operating cost of an assistant that handles 10 million requests a day and averages 1.4 model calls per request, as in the repeated-search example of Chapter 13. Each call has a 1,200-token prompt and a 300-token response. Take hypothetical prices of $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens, which are not any provider’s prices but are chosen to make the arithmetic easy to check.

Now every design decision has a price. Trimming the prompt by a quarter changes the input term. A retry policy that adds ten percent more calls adds more than $11,000 a day. Caching may reduce model invocations, while the latency dashboard alone does not report how much each request costs.

Telemetry has a price as well. The number of time series a metric produces is the product of its label values. A request counter labeled by 12 endpoints, 5 status classes, and 200 instances produces 12,000 series. Add a customer identifier with two million values and the potential count rises to 2.4×10102.4\times10^{10}2.4×1010. Such a metric can become expensive to collect and impractical to query.

Insurance is a cost too. The payment design in Chapter 14 reserves 45 of its 200 provider calls, or 22.5 percent, for captures, reconciliation, and emergencies. That capacity sits idle in normal operation. It is the price of being able to recover, and it should appear in the review as a cost accepted on purpose.
